name: Order of Operations, BODMAS, Brackets and Modulus
description: Simplify expressions in the sequence used by the chapter, including brackets, the bar rule, signs and absolute value.
script_scope: Teach the chapter's BODMAS sequence exactly as stated: brackets first in the order ( ), { }, [ ], then 'of', division, multiplication, addition and subtraction. Use the chapter's repeated-division and mixed-operation examples to show that a learner must simplify the relevant inner or earlier operation before moving outward. Introduce Virnaculum (the bar over an expression) and teach that the part under the bar is simplified before BODMAS. Teach modulus |a| using the chapter's positive and negative examples, plus signed-number multiplication and subtraction where they occur in objective questions. Cover missing-operation traps caused by nested brackets and negative signs. A learner should be able to read a dense expression, mark the next operation, simplify one safe step at a time, and check the final sign and size. Keep general fraction technique in the fractions subtopic and algebraic identities in the identities subtopic.

name: Fractions, Mixed Numbers and “of”
description: Simplify ordinary and mixed fractions, reciprocals and fraction-of-a-quantity expressions.
script_scope: Teach the fraction operations repeatedly tested in the chapter: convert mixed numbers to improper fractions when needed; add and subtract using a common denominator; multiply with cancellation before multiplication; divide by multiplying by the reciprocal; and interpret 'of' as multiplication, with 'of' handled before division according to the chapter's BODMAS rule. Include compound fraction expressions, fraction comparison by exact arithmetic, finding what fraction one quantity is of another, and simple missing-fraction equations. Emphasize that cancelling is allowed only across multiplication, not across addition or subtraction. Include objective-style expressions where several fractions, 'of', division and mixed numbers occur together. A learner should be able to simplify exactly and preserve the fraction in lowest terms. Leave continued fractions for the nested-expression subtopic and word-based part/remainder modelling for the applications subtopic.

name: Missing Values and Basic Equation Rearrangement
description: Turn question marks into unknowns and undo arithmetic operations without losing the order of the expression.
script_scope: Teach how the chapter handles a missing numeral or missing fraction: replace ? or * with a variable, simplify the known parts, then isolate the unknown using inverse operations. Cover an unknown addend, minuend, subtrahend, factor, dividend and divisor; equations where the unknown sits inside brackets; and equations involving a simple fraction. Show the reverse-operation idea clearly and verify every result by substitution into the original expression. Include the chapter's common trap that an unknown divisor cannot be moved as though it were an addend. A learner should be able to translate a missing-value MCQ into a one-variable equation, solve it in small steps, and reject impossible or duplicate choices. Keep simultaneous equations and ratio-based unknowns in the next subtopic.

name: Ratios, Proportions and Simultaneous Equations
description: Convert ratio information into equations and solve two- or three-variable relationships efficiently.
script_scope: Teach the algebraic relationship patterns used throughout the chapter: turn x/y = a/b into bx = ay; combine chained ratios; substitute one ratio into a linear equation; and solve pairs of linear equations by addition, subtraction or substitution. Extend to the chapter's simple three-variable systems by eliminating one variable at a time. Include cost-of-items and share relationships where two equations are formed from a short statement, plus questions that ask for a combination such as x+y or 5y+7x rather than each variable separately. Teach a learner to look first for the requested combination because sometimes the equations can be combined without solving every variable. Keep quadratic equations in the reciprocal/quadratic subtopic and longer story modelling in the word-equations subtopic.

name: Algebraic Identities and Factorisation Shortcuts
description: Recognize square, difference-of-squares and cube identities so large-looking expressions collapse quickly.
script_scope: Teach and apply only the identities listed or used in the Simplification chapter: (a+b)^2, (a-b)^2, their sum and difference, a^2-b^2, (a+b)^3, (a-b)^3, a^3+b^3, a^3-b^3, (a+b+c)^2, and a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc. Show how to identify the numerator and denominator of a known factorization before multiplying large numbers. Include the special case that when a+b+c=0, a^3+b^3+c^3=3abc, as used in the objective questions. Cover numerical identity questions built from large nearby numbers, symmetric expressions and cancellation after factorization. A learner should be able to name the matching identity, substitute the values, simplify safely and explain why direct multiplication is unnecessary. Keep reciprocal-power identities in their own subtopic.

name: Reciprocal Expressions and Quadratic Relations
description: Use x ± 1/x relationships, symmetric sums and factorised quadratics to avoid solving more than necessary.
script_scope: Teach the recurring objective patterns built from x+1/x and x-1/x. Derive x^2+1/x^2 from squaring, then build x^3+1/x^3 or x^3-1/x^3 using the chapter's cube identities. Teach symmetric two-variable relations such as x+y and xy leading to x^2+y^2 or x^3+y^3. Cover simple quadratic equations solved by factorisation, including the fact that a quadratic can have two valid roots and an MCQ may explicitly allow more than one answer. Include equations that become quadratic after simplification. A learner should know when the requested expression can be found directly from a relationship and when the variable itself must be solved. Do not introduce quadratic formula or theory absent from the chapter.

name: Nested Fractions, Continued Fractions and Telescoping Patterns
description: Work from the deepest layer outward and spot products or sums whose middle terms cancel.
script_scope: Teach finite continued fractions by starting at the deepest denominator and moving outward one layer at a time, as in the chapter's solved examples and objective questions. Include repeated self-similar continued fractions where a variable is introduced for the whole expression. Teach telescoping products such as consecutive factors that cancel after rewriting, and telescoping sums based on 1/[n(n+1)] = 1/n - 1/(n+1), which are repeatedly used in the chapter. Include short patterned series where grouping or cancellation is visible, and explain the difference between a genuine pattern and guessing from the first two terms. A learner should be able to simplify a nested expression bottom-up, expose cancellation explicitly, retain only the surviving end terms, and check the result's size.

name: Defined Operations, Changed Symbols and Rule Machines
description: Follow a definition literally when a question invents a new operator, changes symbols or gives a sequence of steps.
script_scope: Teach the chapter's custom-operation questions: if x*y is defined by a formula, replace the custom symbol with that formula before doing ordinary arithmetic. Cover nested custom operations, piecewise definitions where the rule depends on comparing the inputs, and questions in which +, -, × and ÷ are deliberately reassigned. Include step-machine questions that say Step I, Step II and Step III, and special notation whose meaning is defined inside the question. Emphasize that the given definition overrides the symbol's usual meaning and that nested operations must be evaluated from the inside out. A learner should be able to rewrite the expression in ordinary arithmetic, keep each temporary result visible, and avoid carrying the invented symbol into later steps.

name: Numerical Shortcuts, Cancellation and Approximation
description: Simplify large numerical expressions by cancelling, grouping and rounding only when the question allows it.
script_scope: Teach efficient numerical simplification patterns used in the chapter: cancel common factors before multiplying, group repeated factors, use the distributive law around convenient bases such as 999 or 1000, and rewrite mixed numbers close to a whole number when it shortens multiplication. Reuse chapter identities when a large numerical numerator/denominator is clearly built to factor. Cover decimal arithmetic and the later objective questions that explicitly ask for an approximate value: round each awkward number to a nearby convenient value, preserve the rough scale, then choose the nearest option. Distinguish exact simplification from approximation and never round when the question asks for an exact value. A learner should be able to choose between cancellation, grouping, identity and rounding, and perform a quick magnitude check.

name: Parts of a Whole, Units and Proportional Scaling
description: Translate fractions, unit conversions and direct or inverse scaling into short equations.
script_scope: Teach the chapter's fraction-of-a-whole applications without expanding into later dedicated topics. Cover finding the whole from a known fraction, finding a requested fraction of the whole, successive fractions of the remainder, and comparing two fractional parts. Include unit conversions used in the chapter: feet/inches, metres/centimetres, litres, time fractions and currency subunits. Teach direct scaling through unit rate and equivalent ratios, such as marks converted from one total to another or cost for a changed quantity. Teach inverse scaling where a fixed total is filled by containers of different capacity. A learner should be able to choose a common unit, write the part-whole equation, identify whether the relationship is direct or inverse, and attach the correct unit to the answer.

name: Linear Word Equations: Costs, Counts, Rates and Distribution
description: Model everyday chapter problems with one or two linear equations instead of trial and error.
script_scope: Teach the major linear story patterns from the chapter: two-item cost equations, equal distribution where the number of people changes, correct/wrong answer scoring, heads-and-legs counting, equal-value coin denominations, and simple catch-up or reading-rate equations. Show how to name the unknown, translate one sentence at a time, preserve units, and check the solution against every condition. Include the useful shortcut of subtracting a baseline case, such as treating every animal as two-legged before counting extra legs, or every coin as the lower denomination before counting extra value. A learner should be able to distinguish one-equation and two-equation stories, solve them cleanly and reject answers that violate a count or money condition. Do not teach full time-work or time-distance theory beyond the arithmetic relationships shown here.

name: Sequential Change, Reverse Working and Repeated Cycles
description: Handle problems where a quantity changes in stages, repeats in cycles or must be reconstructed from the end.
script_scope: Teach the chapter's multi-stage arithmetic puzzles: passengers or items are repeatedly removed and added, quantities double between stages, or a fixed fraction plus a constant is taken each time. Show when working backward from the final amount is simpler and how to reverse each step in the opposite order. Cover repeated gain/loss cycles such as climb-and-slip or regular withdrawal/deposit patterns, with special attention to the final cycle where the last loss may not occur. Include rows, trees or fence-post questions where n objects create n-1 gaps when both ends are occupied; regular time/day cycles; page-number digit counting by digit blocks; and simple repeating remainder patterns in powers. A learner should be able to draw a stage table, reverse operations safely, separate complete cycles from the final partial cycle, and count intervals rather than endpoints when required.

name: Sets, Overlaps and Inclusion-Exclusion
description: Count people or objects in overlapping groups without double-counting shared members.
script_scope: Teach the set relationships stated in the chapter for two sets: n(A∪B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A∩B), along with only-A, only-B and neither. Use concrete groups such as tea/coffee or languages. Extend the same region-counting idea to the chapter's three-group objective questions: separate only-one, exactly-two and all-three regions before adding; when pairwise counts include the all-three group, subtract it once to obtain the exactly-two region. Include questions that ask for at least two groups, no group, or a missing overlap, and the amusement-park style weighted-count problem where total receipts equal total rides taken. A learner should be able to sketch the regions, place the most specific overlap first, avoid double counting, and check that all regions add back to the stated total.
